queue.tree_name: The Becks Prime Augusta Live Oaks
queue.recognise: You can recognise them by the limbs propped up on wooden stilts, with the drive-through lane running under the canopy. They stand behind the Becks Prime restaurant at 2615 Augusta Drive.
queue.story:
Most restaurants buy land for the parking. The owners of this Becks Prime bought theirs in 1988, by a local news account, mainly for the trees. Two live oaks stand behind the building on Augusta Drive, each reported at about 70 feet tall, and the Heritage Society, Houston's history museum, estimates the oak it names at 400 to 500 years old. Another account has them sprouting around the 1620s. Neither figure comes with a ring count or a girth, so read both as estimates. Even the low end has these oaks standing well before Houston was founded in 1836.

queue.recognise: A tall, straight-trunked pecan standing well clear of the trees around it, on the short trail that carries its name.
queue.story:
There is a footpath in Sugar Land called Old Pecan Tree Trail, and it is named after exactly what you would hope. The tree is a pecan of 467 centimetres round and twenty eight metres tall, with a crown spreading twenty five metres, measured by the Texas A&M Forest Service in March 2026. Trail guides rank it among the twenty five largest trees in Texas, which is scored on trunk, height and crown together.

Pecan is the state tree, and it is one of the few state trees anywhere chosen for something other than looks: it feeds people. A tree this size drops a serious crop, and in a good year the ground beneath it is worth walking slowly across in October.

The trail is short, well under a kilomet
queue.name: The Old Pecan Tree

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the buttressed trunk, more than 30 feet round, and the white sign that marks it. It stands on the lawn at Jackson Square, beside the courthouse on Whitehead Street.
queue.story:
The trunk of the Kapok Tree on Whitehead Street measures more than 30 feet around, and with its buttresses that figure is a floor, not a ceiling. It stands on the lawn at Jackson Square beside Monroe County's historic courthouse, and a white sign marks the spot, in case the size does not.

Its birth year depends on who you ask. WLRN, reporting in 2024, says a kapok was planted at Jackson Square in 1900. Another account puts the planting at 1905, but we could not read that survey ourselves, so treat those five years as an open question. Either way, the Florida Keys tourism board's estimate of more than a hundred years holds.

It has spent that century next to the county's courthouse. When WLR

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the healed frost cracks ridging its trunk, 3.51 metres round. It stands east of the access road among the marked champion trees, with a white ash, an Austrian pine and a ginkgo.
queue.story:
John Rhodes brought this bald cypress north from Estherwood, Louisiana, and planted it by his farmhouse in Kenosha County. A 1962 caption from the Wisconsin Historical Society says it came in the mid-1800s. The farm later became Bong Air Base, and that ground is now Richard Bong State Recreation Area, where the cypress stands beside the access road with a white ash, an Austrian pine and a ginkgo.

Bald cypress is a southern swamp tree, and Wisconsin winters let it know. The book Every Root an Anchor, published by the Wisconsin Historical Society in 2005, records that its trunk cracked audibly in hard cold and healed over each time, leaving ridges where the wounds closed.

queue.name: The Rhodes Bald Cypress

queue.recognise: You are looking for three yews, not the four Wordsworth counted. The largest is 7.5 metres round, more than the other two combined, and its crown is hollowed. The grove is fenced against sheep above Seathwaite.
queue.story:
William Wordsworth called them "those fraternal Four of Borrowdale, joined in one solemn and capacious grove," and for two centuries visitors have climbed the Cumbrian hillside above Seathwaite looking for exactly that number. They will find three. The fourth yew died at some point nobody recorded, its sex and its story lost with it.

The largest survivor, dated by dendrochronology to roughly 1,500 years old, measures about 7.5 metres round, more than the other two combined. queue.name: The Borrowdale Yews (the Fraternal Four)

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its straight, century-old cypress trunk, just over 5 metres round and about 28 metres tall. It stands inside Parque Espana in Roma Norte, planted the day the park opened in 1921.
queue.story: This tree has a birthday, which on this page is rare. It went into the ground on 21 September 1921, the day Parque Espana was inaugurated for the centenary of Mexican independence, and it has been growing in the same spot in Roma Norte ever since. Almost every other protected tree in Mexico City is dated by legend, by estimate or not at all. This one has a date somebody wrote down. A century of city has happened around it. The Roma was still a young neighbourhood of new houses when the park opened; the 1985 earthquake brought several of them down within a few streets of here; the district emptied and refilled and became the part of town everyone now has an opinion about. queue.recognise: A tall dawn redwood in orange autumn colour beside a gravel path, ivy climbing its trunk.
queue.story:
A dawn redwood stands on a lawn of the Préfargier park in La Tène, and a reader photographed it in its autumn colour, the whole crown burnt orange against a pale blue sky. They named it a métaséquoia, the French name for Metasequoia, and gave a girth of 250 centimetres.

The photograph shows a straight trunk with ivy climbing it, a broad crown of fine feathery leaves and a dark evergreen conifer behind it that makes the colour stand out. A gravel path runs along the bottom of the frame. The dawn redwood sheds its needles each year, which is unusual for a conifer, and the orange phase lasts only a few weeks.

We found no register entry or planting date, so the girth is the reader's figure. Th
queue.name: Métaséquoia in La Tène

queue.recognise: A huge tent of drooping beech branches on an open lawn, reaching almost to the ground.
queue.story:
Three weeping beeches grow together on a lawn of the Préfargier park in La Tène, and their drooping branches have joined into one huge curtain of leaves that reaches almost to the ground. A reader photographed them in autumn with the single note “3 hêtres pleureurs”, three weeping beeches.

In the photograph the mass of leaves is many times the height of the visitor who stands under its edge, green with yellow and gold at the tips. Behind it the other trees are in orange autumn colour.

We found no register entry, girth or planting date, so this page gives none. A weeping beech is a cultivated form of the common beech, grown for its hanging shoots, and it grows into just this kind of tent.
queue.name: A tree in La Tène

queue.recognise: A tall dark giant sequoia with a straight trunk, standing on the lawn in the Préfargier park.
queue.story:
A giant sequoia stands on the lawn of the Préfargier park in La Tène, far from California, and a reader measured its girth at 705 centimetres. They photographed it twice, once from a distance and once close to the trunk.

The photograph shows a tall tree with one straight trunk, blue-green foliage in drooping sprays and a crown that narrows toward the top. The species is the reader's; we could not confirm it from the frame. We have found no register entry, planting date or height for it, so the girth is the reader's figure too. Seven metres round would be a large trunk for a tree in a European park.

queue.recognise: A wide dome of yellow-green lime leaves with many upright shoots, ivy on its trunk, in front of an old garden wall with a brick fountain niche.
queue.story:
A large-leaved lime stands near the wall of the Préfargier park in La Tène, and a reader photographed it in late autumn when its leaves had turned yellow-green. They named the species and gave no measurements.

The crown is a wide, even dome, so full that it hides most of its own branches, and many slender stems rise straight up from the main limbs as if the tree had been cut back to a stool long ago. Ivy climbs the trunk. Behind it stands an old garden wall with a small brick fountain niche, and to the right the shuttered pale walls of a house.

queue.name: Large-leaved Lime in La Tène

queue.recognise: A broad, many-limbed oak standing alone in a grassy clearing, a waymarker post beside its trunk.
queue.story:
Elleholmseken stands alone in a clearing near Elleholm in Blekinge, Sweden, a broad pedunculate oak whose crown spreads in a wide dark web of branches. A reader photographed it in spring, when the first leaves were only a green haze on the twigs, and gave us a girth of 785 centimetres and an age of 300 years.

Their note is in Swedish. “På eken växer rödlistade arter som gammalekslav, grå skärelav och matt pricklav. Vissa år syns också oxtungsvampens fruktkroppar.” In English, red-listed species grow on the oak, among them old-oak lichen, a grey lichen and a dull pin lichen, and in some years the fruiting bodies of the beefsteak fungus show on it.

queue.recognise: A wood of short, thick pollarded oaks, their crowns sprawling from high stubs, standing in bracken with a path through them.
queue.story:
A reader walked into an oak wood at Wantisden in Suffolk and sent us a photograph from among the trunks. Short, thick, twisted oaks stand in a sea of bracken, many of them with a broad base and a crown of sprawling limbs set high on a stub, the shape of trees that were cut for wood long ago.

The reader's note is the story. “There are 4,000 oak trees at this location. Early in their lives they were pollarded, and so now they have an amazing appearance.” They put the age at 400 to 800 years. We have found no survey that counts these trees or dates them, so the number of trees and the age are theirs, and a pollard that old is hard to date without a tape and a core.

queue.recognise: A very thick, knobbled London plane splitting into several stout stems, standing in a raised ivy bed at the edge of a gravel car park.
queue.story:
A reader stopped at a huge London plane on the western edge of Maidstone and wrote that it is “a type of Baobab London Plane tree that must be at least 200 years old. The scale of it in person is jaw dropping.” They gave a girth of 700 centimetres and an age of 250 years.

The photographs show why. The trunk splits close to the ground into a few thick, knobbled stems, each wider than a person, and the bark is dark and burred where it is old and flaking pale where it is not. Above them the limbs fork again and again into a high leafy crown. The tree stands in a raised bed of ivy at the edge of a gravel car park, a low block wall around its foot and a floodlight fixed to one limb.

queue.story:
A reader photographed a great pedunculate oak in an open field on Clingoe Hill in Greenstead, on the east side of Colchester. Their app listed it as an oak near Mistley, but the GPS fix puts it in Colchester, and we have placed it there. They gave a girth of 600 centimetres and an age of about 300 years.

The photograph shows a tree that fills the frame. The crown is a full, rounded dome of dark green leaves, and under it a short, wide trunk with deep hollows and burrs at head height. Two people stand at its foot, one with arms spread wide against the bark, and they look small. The grass around it is dry and pale, the crown still green, so the picture was taken in a dry late summer.

queue.recognise: A tall ginkgo in the garden beside the campus library, its two crowns turning one bright yellow in autumn.
queue.story:
A ginkgo in the garden of the library at the Carmarthen campus of the University of Wales Trinity Saint David turns a deep gold each autumn, and a reader sent us a photograph of it in the rain. The library has large glass windows that look onto the garden, and the reader says that in autumn the tree “shines its glory through those windows.”

In the photograph two crowns rise together out of one mass of leaves, every one the same bright yellow, against a grey sky. A white balcony and a slope of roof sit at the left edge of the frame, the grass below is green, and a few leaves are already on the ground.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its huge low, spreading crown, shading a quarter acre, whose branches rest on the ground rather than reaching upward, on a trunk about 7.8m round. It stands within its own fenced park on Johns Island.
queue.story:
The souvenirs say 1,500 years. The city that owns the tree says 300 to 400, and an academic estimate stretches it to 500. That gap is not carelessness, it is live oak. The species grows fast when young, slows unpredictably and rots out from the middle while the crown is still healthy, so there is no core to pull and nothing to count. What can be measured is girth, and every estimate that starts from the tree itself lands in the hundreds of years rather than the thousands.

queue.recognise: A vast furrowed redwood trunk with burls and a dark hollow near the base, a wooden railing at the bottom right.
queue.story:
"This is the Methuselah tree, a local landmark on the San Francisco Bay peninsula," a reader wrote. "Nearly 2,000 years old, 44 feet around. Easily accessible from Skyline Boulevard." Their photograph shows the base, a vast reddish trunk with deeply furrowed bark, burls and a dark hollow, rising out of green redwood sprays.

The reader linked a Peninsula Open Space Trust article on old-growth redwood, which we could not open, so the figures here are theirs. Forty-four feet is about 13.4 metres. It stands in the churchyard of St Cuthbert's at Doveridge in Derbyshire, and the photograph shows how the village looks after it, with a new oak frame carries the path under its lowest limbs, so that you walk beneath a roof of twisting red-brown branches, with the broad, fluted trunk standing just beyond the posts.

Wikipedia's page for Doveridge gives no age or girth for the tree. Its only mention is a legend that Robin Hood and Maid Marian were married under the old yew in the churchyard, and it says the church itself is more than nine centuries old. The 1,400 years is the reader's figure, and no

queue.recognise: A huge split yew trunk behind black iron railings beside the path, with a wooden information board on the fence.
queue.story:
A reader labelled this yew "near Wilmington" and gave it a girth of 1,030 centimetres and an age of 4,000 years. The pin they dropped lies in the churchyard of St George's at Crowhurst in East Sussex, and the photograph fits, with a huge, split, rust-red trunk behind iron railings, with an information board at the fence.

Wikipedia says the tree's age is uncertain, with estimates from 1,300 to 4,000 years, and that the railings and steel wires keep it from collapsing. A legend says the Reeve of the Saxon King Harold was hanged from it for refusing to reveal where Harold's treasure lay. We have found no measurement of our own, so the girth and the top end of the age are the reader's.

queue.tree_name: The Twisted Sweet Chestnut of Greenwich Park
queue.recognise: A twisted, hollowed chestnut trunk with a broad rounded crown, beside a tarmac path on open grass.
queue.story:
A reader sent this sweet chestnut from Greenwich Park with an age of 360 years, and its twisted, split trunk in low autumn sun explains the interest. The trunk spirals and opens into a hollow, with a rounded crown of gold leaves above it, standing beside a tarmac path on open grass.

The reader tells how Charles II, after taking the throne in 1660, set out a grand plan for the park and planted formal avenues of trees in the French style, and that many of those trees still stand. Sweet chestnut was a common choice for such avenues in the park, but we have no record naming this individual tree as one of them, and the 360 years is the reader's estimate rather than a count. queue.recognise: A very wide, hollow oak trunk inside a low fence on open farm grass, the crown spreading from the top of the barrel.
queue.story:
A reader sent us this oak with a girth of 1,330 centimetres and an age of 1,000 to 1,300 years, and the photograph shows why. The trunk is a vast, hollow barrel of dark ridged bark, with the crown rising from it like a green dome and a fence set back to keep feet off the roots.

It stands at Bowthorpe Park Farm in Manthorpe, near Bourne in Lincolnshire. Wikipedia gives its circumference as about 13 metres, which makes it the second widest individual tree in Britain, behind the Marton Oak in Cheshire.
